concept.name: Token burn
concept.definition: A token burn is the permanent, verifiable removal of tokens from supply by sending them to an unspendable destination or destroying them in-protocol, reducing total supply.
concept.intuition: It is shredding banknotes on-chain: the tokens provably cease to exist, making each remaining token a larger share of the whole.
concept.mechanics: Two forms exist: protocol burns, where issuance rules destroy value automatically (Ethereum burns every transaction's base fee via EIP-1559), and discretionary burns, where projects send tokens to the zero address or a burn() function — often funded by buybacks. Burns are public and auditable, unlike token buyback-and-hold programs.
concept.failure_modes: Burns funded by minting elsewhere (burn-and-mint equilibrium optics) can be theatrics that obscure net issuance; discretionary burn announcements are sometimes used to hype price without changing fundamentals, and burned supply is irreversible if later needed for security budgets.
concept.misconceptions: A burn does not automatically raise price — value accrues only if the burn transfers real economic value (e.g. fee burns) rather than just shrinking a number; burning tokens held by the treasury is accounting, not value creation. Ethereum's base-fee burn is not guaranteed to make ETH deflationary — it depends on burn vs issuance.
concept.example: Since EIP-1559, every Ethereum transaction burns its base fee: at a 20 gwei base fee, a 21,000-gas transfer destroys 0.00042 ETH; over high-demand periods this has burned millions of ETH cumulatively, at times exceeding new issuance.

citations.source: Ethereum.org developer docs - Gas and fees
